newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Steel frame of Indian bureacracy rusting.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Steel frame of Indian bureacracy rusting.

text.p: This spring civil servants in India's biggest state gathered to cast secret votes in a bizarre ballot.
After much nudging, winking and back-slapping, the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officers of Uttar Pradesh chose the three most corrupt officials from their own ranks.
The results were first sealed in a bank locker, then ceremonially taken out and sent to the state's top civil servant, the Chief Secretary, for action.
Nothing has been heard of the results, but some IAS officials who feel corruption is too pervasive want to make the vote an annual event in the hope that the guilty among them will be punished.
Half a century after India inherited its civil service, the "steel frame" of British colonial rule, the words bureaucrat and corrupt have become synonymous.
"VERY IDEALISTIC"
But in the days of the Raj, civil servants were different, says K.B. Lall, who joined the Indian Civil Service in 1938 -- nine years before India won independence.
"When I joined the service, there was no question of corruption," the 81-year-old former bureaucrat says gruffly.
"We were very idealistic," Lall told Reuters in an interview. "Today the steel frame simply doesn't have the same strength, it doesn't inspire the same respect."
When India won freedom from Britain in 1947, half of its people lived in absolute poverty.

Its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, declared economic development his top priority and, borrowing liberally from Soviet socialism, funnelled resources into building a strong government that would spearhead growth.
But Nehru's centralised planning and the need for businessmen to obtain licences for every conceivable activity quickly spawned a huge and lucrative black-market economy.
Lall, who retired a quarter of a century ago, says the bureaucracy has become bloated and inefficient over the decades, and that the government has done little to pare it.

"In the early years of the IAS, the cream of the Indian student world went into the civil services," he said. "One thought one would have the opportunity to do what one aspired to do as a young man, growing up with the impact of the struggle for independence on our minds.
"Today, the top people are not going in. It's not a bad thing that other professions get the cream, but what is bad is if only the residue goes into the civil services."
YOUNG HOPEFULS

Yet every year, more than 200,000 Indians aged 21 to 28 take the entrance test to join the IAS elite. Many sit for it as many as four times, turning down private-sector job offers and studying for up to 16 hours a day for the annual examination that is lightly referred to as the national pastime.

Manisha Mishra, a 23-year-old who has taken the exam twice, says IAS cram schools are packed with not only liberal arts students -- the traditional hopefuls -- but also business school graduates and engineers.

Mishra says the candidates are not driven by idealism or a willingness to sacrifice wealth for the power that the IAS bestows. "It's not as if they're foregoing money for power when they join the government instead of a multinational corporation. That's what is sad about it."
After more than 30 years in service, an Indian bureaucrat gets paid about 20,000 rupees ($560) a month -- roughly the salary of a fresh recruit from a second-rate business school.

But, in deference to the levers of power that he controls even six years after India began dismantling a state stranglehold over its economy, a young IAS bridegroom commands a dowry of hundreds of thousands of rupees.
Dowries are just the tip of the money iceberg. Senior bureaucrats are reputed to be showered with money and gifts for getting an industrialist's file to move through the licence labyrinth.
"A government servant can never be paid enough these days," Lall says. "It's the availability of easy money that draws them to the civil services."
FOCUS ON DEVELOPMENT
Bespectacled, balding and dressed in a beige Nehru-collared safari suit, Lall says working with the colonial rulers was often difficult for bright, young Indians fed on a diet of nationalism.
"The difference between working with Panditji (Nehru) and with the British was that with Nehru the focus was on development and not on maintaining law and order," he said.

"When you were responsible for law and order, there was always a feeling on the part of the (British) bosses that people like K.B. Lall cannot be fully trusted. But they were also very fair. There were inquiries and allegations, and I did not suffer."
Lall, who says he sat for the entrance examination because his father wanted him to, says he dealt with containing the 1942 Quit India movement led by Mahatma Gandhi.

The movement marked the final phase of India's independence campaign. Gandhi was imprisoned and went on a protest fast in jail. Hundreds of thousands of his supporters gave themselves up for arrest in a series of civil disobedience demonstrations.

"It was an ethical problem. Many people thought of resigning, I know I did, and many did resign. When the British government decided to let Gandhiji die in jail, I thought I couldn't comply with those instructions.
"But it wasn't necessary to resign because they withdrew those instructions. One was not really tested," says Lall.
"The key strength of the steel frame was that decisions were taken in the interests of administrative efficiency. Today, it has become different."
($1 = 35.7 rupees)
